children: By Libby George

Fundraising for private credit funds focused on developing economies more than doubled in the first half of 2026, industry data showed, although economic and geopolitical uncertainty slowed dealmaking.

Data from the Global Private Capital Association showed fundraising for emerging market private credit reached $8.7 billion in the first half compared with $3.6 billion a year earlier, and close to the $11 billion raised in all of 2025.

Jeff Schlapinski, GPCA's managing director of research, said strong inflows could continue due to "sustained LP interest in private credit strategies targeting growth markets, particularly Asia," referring to pension funds, insurers and other institutional investors that provide capital.
However, GPCA's data also showed deal activity slowed, which Schlapinski attributed to a more uncertain global backdrop.
"Credit conditions are uncertain globally due to continued inflation risks, trade tensions and geopolitical conflicts," he said.
REASSESSING EMERGING MARKET RISKS

GPCA, which represents about 300 private investors managing $2 trillion of assets, recorded 215 deals worth $6.7 billion in the first half. That compares with 373 deals worth a record $22.5 billion in 2025 and $11.8 billion in the first half of last year.
Private credit, in which investment funds lend directly to companies and projects, has expanded rapidly as banks have retreated from some forms of lending.

The asset class has grown to about $3.5 trillion globally over the past two decades, according to the Alternative Investment Management Association, though less than 10% is invested in emerging markets.
Investment firm Ninety One said the value of deals it facilitated reached $2.1 billion in the 18 months through June, up 40% from the previous period.
"Eighteen months to two years ago, this was complete missionary work ... it was very creative fundraising," Nazmeera Moola, Ninety One's chief commercial officer, private markets, told Reuters.
Moola said the investor base now ranges from development finance institutions to pension and insurance funds, sovereign wealth funds and private investment firms.
Investors are reassessing emerging market risks as geopolitical shifts encourage diversification away from the United States, she said.

More than a third of Ninety One's 90-plus transactions were in infrastructure and real assets, including renewable energy, digital infrastructure and telecoms, mainly in Asian and Latin American countries including India, Brazil and Mexico.

Ninety One plans to launch a $500 million to $1 billion emerging markets infrastructure debt fund by year-end. The International Finance Corporation, Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank and Swedfund have announced commitments to the fund.
Schlapinski said global turmoil was likely to weigh on traditional funding sources for the rest of the year, "which should sustain demand for flexible, tailored private credit solutions."
